processing_steps.method: vacuum induction melting into alloy ingot
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Alloys made of high-purity elements Fe, Mn, Al, C, Be (each 99.99%) and melted into alloy ingots; obtained ingot diameter 60 mm, thickness 30 mm. This is the shared as-cast precursor (proc_as-cast) of the rolled strip.

processing_steps.method: hot rolling (17 passes, two-high mill rolls)
processing_steps.reduction_ratio: 83% of total deformation (plate rolled to 5 mm; 1.5 mm per pass)
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Plate rolled to a thickness of 5 mm by 17 passes at 1050 °C (1.5 mm per roll, strain rate 0.6 s^-1); after each rolling pass the sample was kept in a muffle furnace for 3 min to maintain the rolling temperature.

After the last rolling pass, water cooling was performed until cooled to room temperature. The rapid (water-cooling) cooling rate is contrasted with the slow cooling of the as-cast sample, causing the compound morphology differences.

structures.overall_structure: Hot-rolled (1050 °C) Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C–1.5Be low-density steel: a strongly elongated/banded dual-phase structure consisting of an austenite (γ-Fe) matrix with ferrite (α-Fe/δ) bands elongated along the rolling direction, decorated with dispersed Be–Fe phase (Be11Fe, Be12Fe, Be2Fe) precipitates and Be2C carbides, and containing annealing twins. Increasing Be converts the single γ-Fe rolled structure into a banded α + γ dual-phase structure with dispersed Be–Fe phase.
structures.number_of_phases: 2 main phases (austenite γ-Fe + ferrite α-Fe/δ) plus Be–Fe phase and Be2C precipitates

phases_present.texture: grains elongated along the rolling direction

phases_present.morphology: long light bands strongly elongated/vertically banded along the rolling direction (magenta-arrowed 'α-Fe')
dark particle-rich bands and dispersed spherical/point-like compounds along the rolling direction (blue-arrowed 'Be-Fe phase')

defects.dislocation_density: qualitatively increases with Be content; 1.5Be shows the densest dislocation tangles and cell/wall structures

grain_structure.grain_size_distribution: single dominant area fraction in the 12–13 μm region (≈0.30–0.32), with smaller bars near 5, 7.5 and 25 μm

precipitates.type: Be–Fe phase (beryllium compound; Be11Fe, Be12Fe and Be2Fe identified by XRD of rolled 1.5Be)
precipitates.distribution: dispersed; primarily along grain boundaries and phase interfaces (KAM shows stress concentration at the Be–Fe phase)

precipitates.size: size of Be2C gradually increases with the increase of Be content
precipitates.distribution: both at grain boundaries and within the matrix; elongated shape in 1.5Be

phases_present.morphology: green phase-map matrix; grains with many 1–5° low-angle boundary lines

phases_present.volume_fraction: most ferrite of any panel of the series (large connected red regions)
phases_present.morphology: large connected red ferrite regions in the austenite matrix (phase map)

defects.dislocation_density: densest and most uniformly distributed green/yellow misorientation speckle of the whole series (KAM map of 1.5Be)

grain_structure.grain_size_distribution: grain size of rolled 1.5Be steel is around 13 μm

precipitates.distribution: dense dark precipitates decorating grain boundaries; precipitates concentrated at grain boundary and phase interface

defects.dislocation_density: dense, dark dislocation tangles and cell/wall structures (strong strain contrast); the densest of the 0.5Be–1.5Be series

precipitates.size: Be2C size gradually increases with the increase of Be content
precipitates.distribution: along grain boundaries (GB marked in yellow with red arrows) and in the matrix

defect_interactions.interaction_type: precipitate–grain boundary / phase interface stress concentration
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: KAM shows an evident stress concentration at the precipitation location of the carbide and the Be–Fe phase; the distribution of these precipitates is primarily concentrated at the grain boundary and phase interface. In 1.5Be the stress-concentration distribution is relatively uniform.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: crack nucleation and arrest in dual-phase structure
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: In 1.0Be and 1.5Be dual-phase steels, quasi-cleavage cracks initially occur and rapidly expand inside the grains of the brittle ferrite phase, and are immediately hindered when they expand to the adjacent austenite region with better plasticity; the Be–Fe phase accelerates crack propagation and reduces plasticity.

interfaces.slip_behavior: Under the action of external force a large number of dislocation slip movements and accumulation occur inside the steel; dislocation density increases with Be content (Fig. 16), strengthening the steel. Austenite is destroyed after large plastic deformation.
interfaces.phase_evolution: In the as-cast structure the Be–Fe phase has an 'ancient Chinese character' / needle-like morphology; after hot deformation (rolled 1.5Be) the needle-like compounds decrease evidently and point-like compounds increase, with the distribution changing from aggregate to dispersed; most Be is solubilised into the matrix. When remaining Be cannot dissolve in austenite it precipitates on ferrite as spot-like compounds.
interfaces.interface_notes: EDS of the rolled 1.5Be austenite/ferrite junction shows the inner strip-shaped structure is Mn-rich and Al-rich (ferrite) and the outer strip-shaped structure is Mn-rich and Al-poor (austenite), i.e., the elongated structure is ferrite surrounded by austenite.

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: flat tensile specimen (inset of Fig. 10a; dimensions 50, 20, 10, 6, 3, R5) cut from the rolled sheet by EDM/wire cutting
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Uniaxial tensile test on Instron 5982 universal tester with dynamic extensometer (Instron 2620-601); each data supported by more than three tensile specimens.

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress–strain curve (green, 1.5Be) in Fig. 10(a): rises to just under 1200 MPa and drops at about 15% strain.
strain_hardening_rate: steady-state plateau between ~1.3 and ~2.2 GPa; the 1.5Be (green) curve lies highest and terminates near 15% true strain

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: matrix (austenite) and ferrite of the rolled structure; 15×5 matrix of indents, mean of 25 points
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: FM-ARS9000 Vickers hardness, 500 gf tap force.
Archimedes drainage method; high-precision balance (up to 0.01 g); average of three independently measured density values per sample.
DSC heating curves after homogenisation at a heating rate of 10 °C/min.

comparative_performance.note: The Be steel density is 21.38% lower than that of pure iron while maintaining a high strength-plastic product (Ashby plot, Fig. 20).
Abstract states the Be steel density is about 6.25 g/cm³ with 1.5 wt% Be, ~3.8% lower than the Fe–Mn–Al–C steel (ρ = 6.50 g/cm³) and ~19.87% lower than the commonly used steel grade (ρ = 7.82 g/cm³).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: D/MAX-2500/PC diffractometer, Cu Kα X-ray tube (ASTM: D5380–93[2014])
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: 2θ range 20° to 100°, scanning speed 2°/min, continuous scanning; specimen polished (#150–#800) and ultrasonically cleaned
characterization_methods.purpose: Phase composition of the rolled steel
characterization_methods.key_findings: Rolled 1.5Be shows γ and δ reflections plus Be11Fe and Be2Fe peaks (Be11Fe, Be12Fe, Be2Fe and Be2C reported in the 1.5Be pattern); precipitate peaks grow with Be content.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Axiovert 200 MAT; etched with 8% nitrate alcohol solution, surface finish 0.05 µm
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Sample cut by electric spark; standard metallographic preparation (#400–#5000 sandpaper + 0.5 µm diamond polishing)
characterization_methods.key_findings: Rolled 1.5Be shows a strongly elongated, vertically banded structure with light α-Fe bands, dark Be-Fe-phase bands, γ-Fe matrix and an annealing twin.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Metallographic surface preparation; SEM secondary-electron imaging; EDS element maps of Fe, Mn, C, Al
characterization_methods.purpose: Observe rolled microstructure, austenite/ferrite junction and element distribution
characterization_methods.key_findings: Rolled 1.5Be austenite/ferrite junction; inner elongated (ferrite) region is Mn-rich and Al-rich while the outer region is Mn-rich and Al-poor.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: TEM sample thinned to 40 µm then dual-jet electrochemical polishing in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol at 26.5 V and −20 °C
characterization_methods.purpose: Observe matrix morphology, precipitates, carbides and dislocations
characterization_methods.key_findings: Rolled 1.5Be matrix is austenite (SADP [013], γ-Fe); precipitates are elongated Be2C (SADP [1̄12], Be2C); 1.5Be displays the densest dislocation tangles/cell-walls.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Hitachi S3400 SEM coupled with EBSD; TSL OIM analysis v8 software
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: RD–ND plane; electropolished at −20 °C for 50–65 s at 20 V in perchloric acid + alcohol (1:9)
characterization_methods.purpose: Investigate microstructure, phase distribution, grain structure and KAM
characterization_methods.key_findings: Rolled 1.5Be shows austenite (green) with large connected ferrite (red) regions (most ferrite of the series), grain size ~13 μm, and the densest/most-uniform KAM misorientation.
Rolled/alloy 1.5Be transformation peak at 1154.8 °C; Be addition lowers the transformation temperature (~120 °C decrease vs Be-free).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Instron 5982 universal tester with dynamic extensometer (Instron 2620-601)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Room temperature, initial strain rate 5 × 10⁻⁴ m·s⁻¹, ASTM E8/E8M-16A, >3 specimens per data
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure tensile properties of the rolled sheet
characterization_methods.key_findings: Rolled 1.5Be: YS 941.87 MPa, UST 1201.58 MPa, TE 18.33%.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: 500 gf load; 15×5 matrix, average of 25 points

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: High-precision balance (up to 0.01 g); deionised water (ρ = 1×10³ g/cm³)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Sample fully immersed in water; average of three independently measured density values
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the density of the experimental steel

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Secondary-electron imaging of the fractured tensile specimens (Fig. 12, 50 µm scale bar for 1.5Be)
characterization_methods.key_findings: Rolled 1.5Be fracture surface is comparatively flat with large facets, cleavage-like platforms and 'cleavage steps'; mixed ductile-dimple/cleavage mode (plastic-brittle fracture).

computational_details.simulation_method: Thermodynamic (CALPHAD-type) equilibrium calculation of the Fe–Be binary phase diagram
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: The calculated Fe–Be phase diagram is stated to be consistent with the observed distribution of the Be–Fe phase (no solid solubility in austenite near room temperature; beryllium precipitates as compounds).

computational_details.simulation_method: Analytical atomic size factor / Hume-Rothery model for solid-solution type
computational_details.potential_model_or_database: Atomic radii from the periodic table (Table 5 / Fig. 18)
computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Fe solvent (rA = 124 pm); rule that Δr < 8% with same crystal structure gives an infinite solid solution
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Conclusion: beryllium (111 pm) is not an infinite solid solution in the iron matrix, consistent with Be–Fe compound formation observed in the microstructure.

analytical_models.model_name: Relative atomic size difference Δr = |(rA − rB)/rA|
analytical_models.equation_role: Determine the solid-solution type of solute atoms in the Fe matrix
analytical_models.model_note: Be, Al and Mn form substitutional solid solutions while C forms an interstitial solid solution; Be (smaller than Fe) causes inward lattice contraction/distortion and Al (larger than Fe) causes outward lattice expansion.

unmapped_findings: The rolled 1.5Be (Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C–1.5Be, hot-rolled at 1050 °C) alloy belongs to the dual-phase austenite (γ-Fe, FCC) + ferrite (α-Fe/δ, BCC) group; XRD of the rolled 1.5Be steel reports Be11Fe, Be12Fe, Be2Fe and Be2C peaks (b0036), while Fig. 7 legend keys only Be11Fe and Be2Fe.
Density discrepancy for 1.5Be: the abstract quotes ~6.25 g/cm³ (b0009) while Table 3 (rolled state) gives 6.29 ±0.05 g/cm³ (b0065); b0099 also states 6.29 g/cm³.

DSC peak discrepancy: b0035 quotes a Be-free steel transformation temperature of 1278.8 °C, whereas the Fig. 6 label for 0Be reads 1320 °C (broad peak rising from ~1270 °C). For 1.5Be the printed peak is 1154.8 °C.

The as-cast microhardness Table 2 (Fig. 5) values (0Be/0.5Be/1.0Be/1.5Be austenite 453.31–479.74 HV; ferrite 437.40–452.54 HV; Be–Fe phase 483.50 and 477.16 HV) pertain to the AS-CAST state and NOT to this rolled sample, so they are excluded from the rolled 1.5Be property records.
The grain-size distribution of rolled 1.5Be (Fig. 14d) shows a single dominant bar in the 12–13 μm region (~0.30–0.32 area fraction), consistent with the ~13 μm reported in b0050.

Fracture of the rolled 1.5Be steel is a mixed ductile-dimple/cleavage (plastic-brittle) mode; spherical precipitates ~2 μm were observed at the bottom of dimples in high-Be steels, acting as micropore-crack nuclei (b0069).

The strength-ductility product (Ashby plot, Fig. 20) places the Be steels at the lowest density with a high product; the 0.5Be sample gives the highest strength-ductility product (above the 45 GPa% gridline).
